media.caption: Example of a controlled editorial figure; replace or remove it before review.

media.alt: Flowchart for diagnosing a page missing from Google: verify the exact URL, inspect indexed data, run a live test, check HTTP access, robots and noindex, compare canonicals, verify internal links and sitemap, then evaluate rendering, duplication, and distinct value.
media.caption: Indexing diagnosis follows the pipeline. Confirm the URL, compare indexed and live data, verify access and directives, review canonical selection and discovery, then evaluate why a crawled page was not selected.
media.credit: Rank Builder SEO Research Desk

media.alt: Rows of network equipment and cables in a server room
media.caption: Indexing diagnosis works best when the search pipeline is treated as a connected system rather than a collection of unrelated settings.
media.credit: Photo by Kier in Sight Archives on Unsplash

media.alt: Printed charts, calculator, pencil, and office supplies arranged on a desk
media.caption: The Page Indexing report is most useful as an inventory and pattern-finding tool, not as a single site-health score.
media.credit: Photo by Cht Gsml on Unsplash

media.alt: Open filing cabinet drawer filled with organized paper records
media.caption: A discovered URL is known to Google, but it has not yet been fetched and processed as a page.
media.credit: Photo by Maksym Kaharlytskyi on Unsplash

media.alt: Long archival corridor lined with rows of storage cabinets
media.caption: A crawled page has entered Google’s processing system, but crawling alone does not guarantee selection for the index.
media.credit: Photo by Michael Förtsch on Unsplash

media.alt: Closed metal security door with a combination lock
media.caption: A noindex directive is an explicit instruction not to include the page in search results once the crawler can read it.
media.credit: Photo by Chelaxy Designs on Unsplash

media.alt: Road closed by red and white construction barricades and traffic signs
media.caption: Robots.txt can block the crawler’s route to a URL, but it is not a privacy control or a guaranteed removal method.
media.credit: Photo by Kevin Kandlbinder on Unsplash

media.alt: Row of nearly identical doors along a brick building facade
media.caption: Canonicalization groups similar alternatives and selects one representative URL from the cluster.
media.credit: Photo by Arvin Yuan on Unsplash

media.alt: Gray and white clock against a pale blue background
media.caption: Google has no universal indexing deadline; the useful question is which stage the URL has reached.
media.credit: Photo by Debby Hudson on Unsplash

media.alt: Aerial view of a highway interchange crossing an urban area
media.caption: A redirect changes the route from a requested source URL to a different destination.
media.credit: Photo by Horizon flights on Unsplash

media.alt: Aerial view of roads converging at a large highway interchange
media.caption: Redirect errors become understandable when every hop is recorded rather than hidden behind the final browser location.
media.credit: Photo by Jakub Żerdzicki on Unsplash

media.alt: Empty storefront with glass doors and no merchandise
media.caption: A URL can look structurally open while providing none of the content the visitor expected.
media.credit: Photo by Nick Russill on Unsplash

media.alt: Closed construction-site entrance with a barrier gate and warning notices
media.caption: A correct 404 closes one missing route while still giving visitors a useful way forward.
media.credit: Photo by Andrew Hall on Unsplash

media.alt: Two racks of computing equipment and dense cabling in a technical facility
media.caption: Server errors require tracing the request through every delivery layer rather than blaming the visible page alone.
media.credit: Photo by Eric Stoynov on Unsplash

media.alt: Electronic card reader mounted beside a closed door in an empty concrete stairwell
media.caption: A 401 response is an access decision before it is an indexing problem.
media.credit: Photo by Jakub Żerdzicki on Unsplash

media.alt: No unauthorised access notice on a glass entrance
media.caption: A 403 response often reflects an explicit edge, firewall, application, or origin access rule.
media.credit: Photo by Phillip Flores on Unsplash

media.alt: Two road-work warning signs standing beside a wall
media.caption: The 4xx family contains several distinct operational messages even when search indexing reaches a similar unavailable-content conclusion.
media.credit: Photo by Marcus Lenk on Unsplash

media.alt: Row of identical doors along a brick building facade
media.caption: An alternate URL can remain accessible while one representative URL is selected for the duplicate group.
media.credit: Photo by Arvin Yuan on Unsplash

media.alt: Room filled with rows of filing cabinets
media.caption: When several similar records exist without a declared preference, Google selects one representative for the group.
media.credit: Photo by kimak kimbek on Unsplash

media.alt: Locked gate secured with a chain and padlock
media.caption: A blocked crawler can still know that a destination exists even when it cannot pass through the gate to read the page.
media.credit: Photo by Kouji Tsuru on Unsplash

media.alt: Hand holding an unfolded paper map
media.caption: A sitemap is useful only when Google can reach the exact file and interpret its routes.
media.credit: Photo by Hans on Unsplash

media.alt: Close-up of a mechanical button labeled PRESS
media.caption: Submitting a request can start a process, but the button cannot repair the page or guarantee the result.
media.credit: Photo by Nik on Unsplash

media.alt: Open planner beside an hourglass and clock
media.caption: Aggregate reporting and URL-level processing can update on different schedules.
media.credit: Photo by Cabri Caldwell on Unsplash

media.alt: Directional signpost with arrows toward several destinations
media.caption: Internal links and sitemaps both point toward pages, but they communicate different kinds of information.
media.credit: Photo by Tanya Barrow on Unsplash

media.alt: Magnifying glass resting on a dark textured surface
media.caption: A search operator can inspect part of the picture without exposing Google’s complete index.
media.credit: Photo by Sasun Bughdaryan on Unsplash

media.alt: Laptop screen displaying JavaScript code beside a coffee mug
media.caption: JavaScript pages must survive crawling, rendering, and indexing; a working browser view is only one observation.
media.credit: Photo by Daniil Komov on Unsplash

media.alt: Open laptop with a blank screen on a desk
media.caption: A page can look complete in a familiar browser while a fresh rendering environment receives an empty result.
media.credit: Photo by Jakub Żerdzicki on Unsplash

media.alt: Spiral staircase viewed from above
media.caption: An infinite interface still needs distinct, reachable steps underneath it.
media.credit: Photo by Pascal Meier on Unsplash

media.alt: Empty green warehouse shelving prepared for inventory
media.caption: Crawl capacity matters when the available shelves and the incoming inventory are both large enough to create a real constraint.
media.credit: Photo by lim woojung on Unsplash

media.alt: Padlock and keys resting on a computer keyboard
media.caption: A WordPress noindex can originate in the site setting, a plugin, theme code, or the delivery layer that surrounds WordPress.
media.credit: Photo by Sasun Bughdaryan on Unsplash

media.alt: Rows of similar boxes arranged on retail shelving
media.caption: Shopify stores can expose several usable paths to similar inventory while one URL remains the search representative.
media.credit: Photo by Declan Sun on Unsplash

media.alt: Laptop screen displaying lines of application code
media.caption: A Next.js route can hydrate successfully while its initial response, metadata, or deployed edge behavior remains wrong for search.
media.credit: Photo by Daniil Komov on Unsplash

media.alt: Rack of servers and network equipment in a data center
media.caption: Cloudflare can change routing, headers, status codes, and cache behavior at the edge after application code has finished its work.
media.credit: Photo by Kevin Ache on Unsplash

media.alt: Magnifying glass beside the corner of a laptop
media.caption: The inspector separates observable page signals from the much larger question of whether a search engine has selected the URL for its index.
media.credit: Photo by MJ Duford on Unsplash

media.alt: Aerial view of a multilane highway interchange
media.caption: A redirect chain becomes understandable when every transition, destination, and failure is shown in order.
media.credit: Photo by Jakub Żerdzicki on Unsplash

media.alt: Clipboard, notebook, pen, hourglass, and stationery arranged on a dark surface
media.caption: A useful indexing study begins with a registered protocol, dated observations, and explicit rules for what counts as evidence.
media.credit: Photo by Alexander Kaufmann on Unsplash

media.alt: Laptop displaying charts beside a notebook and mug
media.caption: The baseline records what was measurable before the new indexing corpus had time to influence search performance.
media.credit: Photo by nicoll camacho on Unsplash
